papers.title: A Linear-Size Well-Separated Pair Decomposition for Unit Disk Graphs
papers.abstract: Given a metric space $(X, d)$ a $c$-well separated pair decomposition (WSPD) is a collection of `dumbbell' pairs of subsets $(A, B)$, $A, B\subseteq X$, where the distance between the two sets is at least $c$ times the diameter of each set and every pair of points in $X$ is covered by one such pair. It is known that for a weighted unit disk graph metric of $n$ points, there is a WSPD of size $O(n\log n)$. But it is open whether this bound can be improved to $O(n)$. In this note, we answer this question affirmatively and provide an algorithm that yields a linear-size WSPD for unit disk graphs.

papers.title: An Omnidirectional WECT: Closed-Form Computation of the Directionally Integrated Weighted Euler Characteristic Transform
papers.abstract: The weighted Euler characteristic transform (WECT) and related directional descriptors have become popular, efficiently computable tools for shape analysis across a variety of domains. In practice, however, they are approximated over a finite set of filtration directions, and thus the vectorized descriptor depends on this choice of directions and the rotational orientation of the data. In this manuscript, we formally introduce the directionally integrated weighted Euler characteristic transform (DIWECT), which averages the WECT over all directions $s \in \mathbb{S}^n$ for a weighted simplicial complex immersed in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. A framework for computing the DIWECT exactly, without sampling directions, is outlined: for each simplex, we partition $\mathbb{S}^n$ into the sets of directions in which a given vertex enters the filtration last, and then the DIWECT at height $t$ reduces to measuring intersections of these regions with a set of directions in which the simplex has entered the filtration by height~$t$. We provide implementations for complexes immersed in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$, in which case the problem reduces to computing arc lengths and spherical areas. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that the DIWECT, while resulting in more compact vectorizations, also successfully encodes shape information and discards noise from data orientation. On a barley seed classification task, it outperforms the WECT in every pose except a hand-curated frame, whose advantage disappears under a two-degree rotation error. Compared with averaging the WECT over sampled directions, the DIWECT is often faster at matched accuracy. In one instance, this is upwards of a $50 \times$ speedup on a one-million-cell image with an error of $10^{-3}$.

papers.title: SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding, yet remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning. Recent studies explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. However, these approaches either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme, regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. Through systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion, we find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels (e.g., distance estimation vs. route planning) require geometric representations of different granularities, revealing that fixed fusion cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements. To bridge this gap, we propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations. SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics, and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. Furthermore, we introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse. Gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. Experiments demonstrate that SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaosb-star/SpatialMind.

papers.title: A Reidemeister-type theorem for vineyards
papers.abstract: Closed vineyards record how persistent homology changes along a periodic family of filtrations. Their topology can be surprisingly complicated, with recent work showing that vines may exhibit nontrivial monodromy even in very simple settings, and more generally that every link can occur in a closed vineyard. In this paper, we study how the global topology and structure of a vineyard change when the periodic family of functions changes. We study radial persistence for a generic planar curve $\mathcal{M}$, where an observation point $x\in\mathbb{R}^2$ defines the squared-distance function $d_\mathbb{E}^2 (\cdot ,x)|_\mathcal{M}$. Moving the point $x$ along a closed observation loop $\gamma$ produces a closed vineyard. Utilizing tools from singularity theory, we show that the topology of this vineyard is controlled by the interaction of $\gamma$ with the generalized symmetry set of $\mathcal{M}$, the geometric discriminant formed by the union of focal and symmetry sets. We establish a Reidemeister-type theorem: under a generic deformation of $\gamma$, every topological change in the vineyard is generated by a finite collection of elementary local moves occurring when $\gamma$ passes codimension-two singularities of the generalized symmetry set. Thus, despite the potentially unbounded global complexity of closed vineyards, their evolution is governed by a finite collection of local geometric events. We classify these events and determine the corresponding changes to the vineyard, giving a complete local description of how radial vineyards evolve under generic deformation. In addition, we derive sufficient geometric conditions under which the resulting vineyard has no monodromy and trivial topology. The 2D case already exhibits very rich behaviour, and we conjecture that in fact it captures all possible generic changes in vineyards.

papers.title: First Order Geometry of Equilateral Small Polygons
papers.abstract: We develop a first order calculus based on the geometry of realised diameter graphs for perimeter maximisation among convex equilateral small polygons. Polygon side equalities and active diameter constraints define a linearised feasible cone and an associated equality space. We prove that an equilateral small polygon is a strict local maximiser of perimeter modulo Euclidean motions if a multiplier balance holds with strictly positive active diameter multipliers and the active equality space consists only of infinitesimal Euclidean motions. The proof uses a local Euclidean slice and a geometric limiting argument and requires neither independence of the active constraint gradients nor second order information. As an application, we combine our criterion with validated interval arithmetic to establish strict local maximality for Bingane and Audet's polygons $A_{16}$, $A_{32}$, $A_{64}$ and for reconstructions of their polygons $Z_{32}$ and $Z_{64}$. For each $n\in\{32,64\}$, the perimeter of $Z_n$ is strictly larger than that of $A_n$. Thus, strict local maximisers with different perimeters coexist in the space of convex equilateral small polygons with the same number of sides.

papers.title: Asymptotic Dimension of Persistence Modules of Bounded Presentation
papers.abstract: We compute the asymptotic dimension of spaces of multiparameter persistence modules of bounded presentation under the interleaving distance. The $d$-parameter modules with at most $n$ generators and $m$ relations have asymptotic dimension, and Assouad-Nagata dimension, exactly $d(n+m)$, the number of coordinates of their generator and relation grades, over every field; for two parameters this is $2(n+m)$. The space has continuous moduli, already for two parameters and $n,m\ge2$: over an infinite field it contains, at every scale, infinite uniformly separated families of pairwise non-isomorphic modules with one fibered barcode, so it is not doubling even at a fixed fibered barcode; already for $m\ge1$ it is not coarsely equivalent to a proper metric space. The proof is an induction on the number of distinct grade coordinates: an interleaving small compared with the gaps between these coordinates moves each of them by at most twice its size and preserves the induced grid representation, so the continuous moduli are invisible at large scale. Each class of modules at finite distance therefore embeds coarsely into Hilbert space; for two parameters, $n,m\ge2$ and an uncountable field, a class containing such a family admits no coarse embedding into a separable Hilbert space. Under the two-parameter matching distance, on the space of rank invariants, the asymptotic dimension and the Assouad-Nagata dimension are again $2(n+m)$: slope-one slices pin the grid of grades, and over a grid only finitely many rank invariants occur; on a finite net of $S$ slices the asymptotic dimension is at most $2nS$.

papers.title: Smooth Surfaces via Nets of Geodesics
papers.abstract: We study the reconstruction of smooth surfaces from networks of spatial curves prescribed as geodesics. Motivated by applications in computer-aided geometric design and the perception of three-dimensional shape, we propose a variational approach minimizing the integral of squared Gaussian curvature over surfaces spanning geodesic contours. Using isothermal coordinates, we derive the Euler-Lagrange equation for the conformal factor of the metric and the associated Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. We also consider a biharmonic approximation obtained by linearizing the nonlinear equation. Numerical experiments are performed on four quadrilateral cells of a geodesic network constructed on an ellipsoid. We compute approximate isothermal coordinates, solve the biharmonic boundary-value problem, and compare the resulting curvature with that of the reference surface. These experiments consist of an important step towards a complete framework for the computation of smooth surfaces from geodesic curves.
